title: The eyes weep
hookLine: when his small son Ibrahim died, the Prophet wept: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves (Sahih al-Bukhari)

cards: The house of a blacksmith named Abu Saif. His wife is nursing a little boy named Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.

A companion named Anas remembers going there with the Prophet, who took the child, kissed him and breathed in his smell, the way parents do. Some time later they came again. This time Ibrahim was dying.
And Anas remembers what happened next: the Prophet's eyes began to fill with tears.

teach.b: The report in Sahih al-Bukhari doesn't start with doctrine. It starts with a father holding a child close enough to breathe him in. Before anything is said about death, we're shown love.
A companion named Abdur Rahman ibn Awf is standing there, and he's surprised.
He says something like: you too, O Messenger of God?
As if a prophet should be above tears. The Prophet answers him: this is mercy. In this report, the tears aren't a lapse in faith.
They're a sign of the mercy God puts in human hearts.

teach.h: EYES WEEP, HEART GRIEVES, TONGUE HOLDS.
teach.b: Then comes the line the story is remembered for: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And to the child: O Ibrahim, we are saddened by your parting.
Three parts of a person, each given its job.
The eyes may weep. The heart may grieve. The tongue holds to what pleases God: no cursing fate, no wild words.
For Muslims, patience in grief limits what is said, not whether tears fall.

Look back over the week: Paul taunting death, Francis calling it sister, the old art of letting go, names in a book, every soul tasting death, a dharra of good. And now a father crying over his boy, and calling it mercy.

how: Muslims point to this hadith to show that weeping over the dead is permitted and merciful, while wailing and words of protest against God's decree are discouraged; mourners are encouraged to say the Quran's words that we belong to God and to Him we are returning (2:156).

o: a merchant of Medina who once sold the Prophet his travel cloak
the companion who asked the Prophet why he was weeping that day
the Prophet's little son, whose death brought tears he called mercy

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Prophet held back his tears to show strong faith
his eyes filled with tears, and he called it mercy.
a companion was surprised to see him weep
Abdur Rahman ibn Awf asked, in effect, even you?
in this hadith, grief is limited in what is said, not in tears
the eyes weep, the heart grieves, the tongue says what pleases God.

games.q: you're the Prophet, at your dying son's side. a companion asks why you, of all people, are weeping. what do you say?
games.why: he answers, this is mercy, and adds: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves.

practice: Bring to mind a loss, recent or old, large or small; don't go looking for pain, just let whatever is near come close.
If tears come, let them, and if they don't, that's fine too, but keep the words gentle, even the ones in your own head. If you pray, you can bring the grief to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Ibrahim, the small son of the Prophet Muhammad, whose death made the Prophet's eyes fill with tears he called mercy. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, from the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: truly, the eye weeps.

carryVoice: Your line: this is mercy. Tears and faith can live in the same heart. A week, done.
